Full release notes: **https://danbyte.net/news/v0-16-0**

### New in 0.16.11

Danbyte can now render the config that gets pushed, for a leaf-spine EVPN fabric with multihoming, a provider MPLS core and the files around FRR. This is the first cut against a real 26-router fabric; the fabric routers render identically to what runs, the edge and WAN routers get their models this release and their templates from the field.

#### Added

- **IS-IS timers and LSP settings as fields.** `lsp-gen-interval`, `spf-interval`, `spf-delay-ietf` (all five values or none), `lsp-mtu`, log adjacency changes and `default-information originate` per family live on the instance, and an IS-IS redistribution carries its family and level. The render hands a template the level as FRR spells it (`level-2-only`), so the template keeps no mapping of its own.
- **BGP session capabilities and instance settings.** Extended next-hop (RFC 5549), TTL security (GTSM) and a default-originate policy on a session or peer group; `distance bgp` and multipath relax on an instance. A session whose route-reflector flag comes from its group says so, so a template prints the line once. An internal peer renders with its AS number, the way the running config has it.
- **Ethernet segments.** A multihomed server is one catalog object naming the LAG on each leaf, by a full ESI or by es-id + system MAC, with its DF preference; an interface's page shows the segment it is in, and a fabric-facing port is marked **EVPN MH uplink**. The render carries the segment per port, every member on every device, and a count per leaf.
- **MPLS: LDP and L3VPN.** One LDP instance per provider router - router id, transport address, host-routes-only labels, the interfaces it speaks on - and the four VPN leak settings on a customer VRF's BGP instance; the RD and route targets stay on the VRF.
- **The cable's far end in the render context.** Every interface carries `link_peer` - the peer device, its port, its description and custom fields - so a port description can read `to spine1 Gi3` without reaching a model method the sandbox refuses.
- **Config bundles.** A router is several files, not one: a bundle names the device templates that produce them (each with a target path) and the roles they apply to. `render/?bundle=role` returns every file with its path and hash, or a tarball; `GET /api/devices/render/` does it for every device a filter selects, in one call.
- **What was last pushed.** A push tool records the file it put on a device; from then on every render says whether it still matches (*Matches last push*, *Changed since last push*, *Never pushed*) with a diff against the pushed text, so a model change shows before anyone reads the box.
- **The keychain placeholder is a contract.** A render prints `<keychain:NAME>` where a key belongs, exactly that shape, and the docs say so; a push tool substitutes it from the audited reveal endpoint or its own store.
- **`used_bfd_profiles`** in the render context: only the profiles a device names, so a box with fabric ports alone stops rendering a `wan` profile. The generated OpenAPI schema is cached for an hour.
- **A VM's SNMP tab** lists its ARP table and reads each SNMP interface against the VM's NICs; a guest that names its NIC differently from the hypervisor gets an **SNMP name** on the interface, as device interfaces have. (#98)

#### Fixed

- **A VM renamed on the hypervisor is renamed here.** The name was only read at adoption, so the vApp followed a rename and the VM did not. A rename is now spec drift: applied to a sync-created VM in automatic mode, proposed in review, and refused with a note when the name is already taken. (#98)
- **The source list's Sync button no longer reads as syncing every source.** One shared pending flag turned every row's button into "Syncing…"; each row now reads it against its own source. The request was always per source. (#98)
- **Row permissions cost one query per page, not two per row.** A site-scoped grant always produces a filter, so the per-row lookup was the normal path for exactly those users: 222 queries on a page of 100 devices, now 24. (#218)
